One generalization is a related but distinct sub-pattern about the precision of inline code comments.

text: For RSS/Atom feed item author metadata (e.g., `item_author_name` in `foundation/feeds.py`), set a stable collective/organizational label (e.g., "DSF Board") when authorship varies across items, rather than an individual's name, a dynamic per-term role lookup, or an office title that can change. If role-based attribution is genuinely needed, name the role that actually produces the content (e.g., the Secretary writes the minutes, not the Treasurer) — never a guessed or assumed office.
reason: Prevents incorrect, stale, or misleading attribution in generated feeds as attendees, writers, and board roles change over time, while still crediting the correct responsible role when a role label is used.
common_pattern: Authorship/attribution metadata for generated RSS/Atom feed items: how to choose `item_author_name` so feeds are stable, correctly attributed, and not tied to transient individuals or incorrect office titles.

text: When updating the Django Fellows section in `djangoproject/templates/fundraising/index.html`, keep the historical record complete, accurate, and stylistically consistent: include every current and former Fellow, use plural wording/counts when there are multiple former Fellows, and write each bio with concrete role/start-date and fellowship-end/tenure details matching the existing entries. Verify counts and identities against official announcements when needed.
reason: The fundraising page's Django Fellows history should accurately represent all fellows and follow the established bio format, avoiding incomplete or misleading program history.
common_pattern: Maintaining accurate, complete, and stylistically consistent Django Fellows history content on the fundraising index page.

text: In user-facing templates, documentation copy, and translated strings, follow standard English grammar and style: avoid 'and/or'; use plural verb agreement for compound subjects joined by 'and'; and use a comma before a coordinating conjunction only when it joins two independent clauses, not when it joins a compound predicate.
reason: Keeps public-facing copy clear, grammatical, and consistent across translated and template content.
scope: user-facing templates, translated strings, and documentation prose
common_pattern: User-facing/template copy must follow standard English grammar and style conventions, especially around conjunctions, subject-verb agreement, and punctuation.

text: Member-facing copy in `templates/members/` must accurately describe membership: frame membership as recognition of contributions (not as granting influence over project direction), use a celebratory tone, list all currently active communication channels (including ones no longer used for conversations unless actually retired), and distinguish automatic onboarding from opt-in channels without implying opt-in channels are automatic.
reason: Inaccurate or incomplete membership copy misleads members about benefits, influence, and which channels they will be added to, and omitting still-active channels drops accurate information.
common_pattern: DSF member-facing communications must accurately describe membership benefits, influence, and channel enrollment, and must respect member consent/expectations when sending outreach.

text: When authoring GitHub issue templates under `.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/`, make them clear, visible, and correctly scoped for users: use descriptive, user-facing section headings with standard acronym capitalization (e.g., 'URL'), keep instructions as visible Markdown rather than HTML comments, and include notes that redirect off-topic reports (e.g., translations) to the project's official external/localization resources.
reason: Issue templates are user-facing forms; ambiguous labels, hidden instructions, and missing routing notes make it harder for reporters to submit useful issues and increase maintainer triage burden.
common_pattern: Guidance for authoring GitHub issue templates so they are user-facing, visible, and correctly route off-topic reports: clear headings/labels, visible instructions, and notes directing users to appropriate external workflows.

text: Place explanatory comments immediately above the specific line(s) of code they describe, rather than elsewhere in the block.
reason: A comment separated from the code it explains is harder to associate with the correct line and becomes misleading or ambiguous during refactoring.
common_pattern: Comment hygiene: comments should carry information the code cannot (non-obvious intent, constraints, magic values), be placed with the code they explain, and follow standard syntax. Six of nine generalizations converge on the 'do not restate / do not document change history' half, and one (Gen 7) supplies the complementary 'do document non-obvious magic values' half.

text: Keep docstrings synchronized with the implementation: when a function's return contract changes, update the docstring to describe the new return type and fields; when a function is a simplified wrapper around an upstream library function, explicitly name the upstream function and describe the custom behavior in unambiguous terms.
reason: Prevents misleading documentation and ensures callers understand what is actually returned or how the wrapper differs from the upstream function.
common_pattern: Docstrings must remain accurate and explicit about a function's behavior, especially when its implementation changes or wraps upstream functionality.

text: Write docstrings and comments as meaningful, complete sentences in sentence case: every new function (including custom template tags) should have a non-empty docstring that starts with a capital letter, ends with a period, and avoids title-casing descriptive phrases.
reason: Empty or placeholder docstrings add noise, while consistent sentence-style documentation makes intent discoverable and maintainable, especially for template tags referenced outside their implementation.
common_pattern: PEP 257-aligned docstring and comment style conventions: meaningful presence, complete-sentence capitalization/punctuation, sentence case, and one-line brevity for short descriptions.

text: Use a single-line docstring (`"""Short description."""`) for short or obvious descriptions, and reserve multi-line docstrings for longer descriptions that need a summary line plus body; follow PEP 257.
reason: One-line docstrings keep short documentation concise and reduce unnecessary formatting noise without losing information.
common_pattern: PEP 257-aligned docstring and comment style conventions: meaningful presence, complete-sentence capitalization/punctuation, sentence case, and one-line brevity for short descriptions.

text: Search result links must anchor to the matched section's title/heading, not to the first occurrence of the search term. When a match is inside a section, the link should use the section's own anchor (a fragment derived from the section title/heading) so users land on the relevant section rather than an arbitrary first `<mark>`.
reason: Anchoring to the first highlighted term scrolls users to a disorienting location and conflicts with their expectation that a result title opens the target page at its heading; anchoring to the matched section's heading gives predictable, relevant navigation.
scope: docs search result templates and query layer
common_pattern: Search-result link navigation: result links should target the matched section's own heading/anchor (supplied by the query layer) rather than the first occurrence of the search term, and the template should reuse existing anchor helpers instead of reconstructing link context.

text: Section headings in content/documentation templates must include a permalink anchor appended after the (translated) heading text, of the form `¶` (or `¶`), where the fragment is the slugified version of the heading's own visible text. The anchor `id`/`href` must match the heading text and must be unique across the document — never copy an existing anchor when adding a new heading, and never use a synonym or divergent wording.
reason: Consistent, copyable deep links to individual sections; mismatched or duplicated anchors break in-page linking and mislead users about which section a link targets.
common_pattern: Section headings in site/documentation templates must expose a deep-link anchor whose fragment is the slugified heading text (Django's `plink`/`headerlink` convention), and anchor `id`s must be unique and attached to existing semantic elements rather than empty wrappers.

text: Local development documentation should not instruct users to perform manual setup steps for services or resources that belong in the Docker Compose environment; instead, provision them automatically via Docker Compose/init scripts, and document how each workflow relates to the standard `docker compose up` flow.
reason: Manual setup instructions for containerized local development are error-prone, non-reproducible, and cause Docker environments to diverge from documentation. If a service or resource is part of the local compose setup, it should work automatically when compose is up, and README sections should make their purpose relative to that standard workflow clear.
common_pattern: Local Docker Compose development environments should automatically provision required services and resources via `docker compose up` / init scripts; documentation should avoid manual setup instructions and clearly explain how each documented workflow relates to the standard compose workflow.

text: Curated ecosystem/package lists should include only actively maintained, mature projects; if a package is deprecated or recommends a successor, list the successor instead.
reason: Curated lists should not promote unmaintained or deprecated packages, especially when upstream explicitly recommends migration.
common_pattern: Curated third-party resource listings and documentation links should direct users to authoritative, current, user-facing project destinations and avoid stale, unofficial, or unmaintained entries.

text: When creating a new content/page template by copying an existing one (e.g., a statement, policy, or code-of-conduct page), audit every block explicitly: keep all required content, including short sections such as feedback invitations, and drop boilerplate (shared sidebar, legal, or license blocks) that the new page does not uniquely need.
reason: Blind copying produces incomplete pages when content is dropped and duplicated maintenance burden when unrelated boilerplate is carried over; an explicit per-block audit prevents both failure modes.
scope: content/template creation by copying an existing document
common_pattern: Both rules concern the content curation of a new document/template created by porting an existing one: one warning against under-inclusion (dropping required paragraphs) and the other against over-inclusion (copying irrelevant boilerplate). They are complementary halves of a single principle: deliberately audit every block when duplicating a template.

text: In documentation and user-facing templates, make calls-to-action solicit contributions as frictionlessly and invitingly as possible: link directly to the actionable target (e.g., the GitHub 'edit file' URL for that document) rather than only saying 'submit a pull request', and phrase feedback requests around the benefit to the reviewing body ('would benefit from your feedback') rather than the body's ability to use it ('can use your feedback').
reason: Direct links remove friction, and reader-centered phrasing is more inviting and less utilitarian — together they maximize the likelihood readers actually respond to the call-to-action.
scope: documentation contribution instructions and user-facing copy
common_pattern: Optimizing documentation calls-to-action: minimizing reader friction (direct edit-file links) and using reader-centered, benefit-focused phrasing — both aimed at making it as easy and inviting as possible for readers to contribute feedback or edits.

text: In user-facing documentation and templates, use active voice and name the responsible role or team explicitly instead of passive voice or vague actors such as 'someone'.
reason: Active voice and named actors improve clarity and accountability, making it clear who performs an action and whom readers can contact.
common_pattern: User-facing documentation and template copy should make the responsible actor explicit and use active voice rather than passive constructions or vague actors.

text: When documenting exploratory packages or features that seek community feedback, explicitly list the specific aspects under evaluation (for example, API design or multi-backend compatibility) instead of providing only a generic package summary.
reason: This focuses reviewers and the community on the key open questions being evaluated, making feedback more actionable.
common_pattern: Documentation for exploratory or experimental packages should explicitly identify the specific aspects on which community feedback is sought, rather than giving only a generic package summary.

text: When documenting translation/locale directories in a multi-site repository README, each locale path bullet should identify the target site/domain and clarify whether the files translate the app/site UI rather than documentation content.
reason: Prevents readers from confusing application/site translation files with translation files for documentation content.
common_pattern: Both sub-patterns concern Django localization configuration: one about avoiding redundant LOCALE_PATHS settings (since Django auto-discovers app locales), the other about disambiguating locale directories in documentation for multi-site repos. They share the domain (Django translations) but address distinct concerns (settings config vs. README documentation), so they form two complementary sub-patterns rather than one unified rule.

text: In member invitation emails, state that the account name should match the external service username (e.g., GitHub username used for Trac), and tell recipients they can request a correction if there is a mismatch.
reason: Prevents broken profile integrations and contribution statistics, while giving users a recovery path when account details are admin-controlled.
common_pattern: Invitation emails for member accounts should proactively explain the external-username matching requirement and provide a recovery path for mismatches.

text: In comments, docstrings, and help text, reserve `user` for instances of the `User` model; refer to human account holders as `person` (or another distinct term) to avoid ambiguity.
reason: `User.profile` is a 1:1 relation and `trac_username` is singular, so using `user` to mean both the model instance and the real person makes documentation ambiguous.
common_pattern: Terminology disambiguation in code comments/docs: reserve the term `user` for the `User` model instance and use a distinct term (e.g. `person`) for the human/account-holder entity, to avoid overloading a loaded word.

text: When a template link becomes stale — because its target URL moved, the section was renamed, or the link is broken — update the link rather than deleting it: repoint the `href` to the new canonical destination and update the visible label to match the current terminology, keeping the label wrapped in `{% translate %}`.
reason: Stale links still point readers to useful information; removing them loses discoverability of content that exists elsewhere on the site, while correct labels and translation wrappers keep the UI accurate and localizable.
common_pattern: Maintaining links in templates when their targets move or are renamed: update the link (href and/or visible label) to reflect the new canonical destination rather than deleting it, while keeping user-facing labels translatable.

text: When editing factual prose in user-facing documentation or templates, especially under `djangoproject/templates/`, verify every claim (dates, names, tenures, where information is published, etc.) against the authoritative linked source before committing. Do not infer facts from surrounding text, URL slugs, or nearby content; correct the copy if the claim is false.
reason: Inaccurate user-facing documentation misleads users, and inferred facts can silently contradict the authoritative source.
common_pattern: Factual claims in user-facing documentation/templates must be verified against the authoritative source before being written or edited, rather than inferred from context or assumed to be correct.

text: In public-facing ecosystem/documentation pages, use descriptive, accurate, framework-neutral section headings that clearly name the full range of content and avoid project-specific jargon or misleading labels.
reason: Accurate and neutral headings set correct user expectations, help users from other ecosystems understand the content, and prevent misleading impressions about what a section contains.
common_pattern: Section headings in public-facing documentation and ecosystem pages should be descriptive, accurate, and framework-neutral, clearly communicating the full scope of the section's content without misleading labels or project-specific jargon.

text: Standalone scripts in `tools/` must begin with a module docstring that documents: the script's purpose, a Usage line showing the invocation, each command-line argument with a concrete example value (e.g. `<YYYY-MM>` example `"2023-04"`), and a Behavior section listing what the script does and where it writes output.
reason: Makes the CLI contract and side effects (especially output paths) self-documenting without reading the argparse setup or the script body, and example values clarify expected formats that flag names alone do not convey.
common_pattern: Documentation and CLI-interface conventions for standalone tooling scripts: module docstrings that document purpose, usage, arguments (with example values), and behavior, plus required argparse options that feed parsed values into the generation function rather than hardcoding inputs.

text: When documenting a duration, count, or date offset (in docstrings or inline comments), state the reference point explicitly — e.g., '28 months of extended support beyond mainstream' or 'after mainstream ends' — rather than an ambiguous 'total' or an unstated base date. Use the same wording in the comment as the calculation uses.
reason: An ambiguous phrase like '28 months total extended support' can be misread as the overall support lifetime rather than the amount appended after mainstream support; naming the base point removes the ambiguity without adding length and keeps comments consistent with the underlying date arithmetic.
common_pattern: Both generalizations address the same underlying ambiguity problem: when documenting a duration, count, or date offset (in docstrings or inline comments), the reference point must be named explicitly rather than left implicit (e.g., 'total', 'from release date'). Docstrings and inline comments are complementary contexts for the same rule.

text: In release/setup checklists and runbooks, command snippets that invoke repository scripts must explicitly state the working directory and keep script paths consistent with directory navigation: either run from the repository root using a `scripts/` prefix (e.g., `VERSION={{ release }} scripts/verify_release.sh`) with no contradictory `cd ..`, or `cd scripts` first, invoke the script without the `scripts/` prefix, and `cd ..` to restore. Avoid ambiguous phrasing like 'from `scripts` folder' that conflates script location with working directory.
reason: Prevents contradictory instructions that cause users to run commands from the wrong working directory, and removes ambiguity about whether a script is located in `scripts/` or should be run while inside `scripts/`.
common_pattern: Command snippets in documentation checklists/runbooks must have internally consistent working-directory semantics: state the intended working directory explicitly, and make script path prefixes (e.g., `scripts/`) consistent with any `cd` navigation so instructions are unambiguous and runnable.

text: Wrap prose lines in documentation and markdown/reStructuredText source files to a fixed column width (about 79–90 columns), matching the existing line-wrapping convention of the file when one is present.
reason: Keeps prose fully visible without horizontal scrolling in narrow editor/split-pane layouts and keeps documentation diffs stable by avoiding reflow churn.
scope: documentation files (markdown / reStructuredText); global default with per-file override to match existing convention
common_pattern: Both generalizations require wrapping prose lines in documentation/markdown source files at a fixed column width for readability and diff stability, differing only in the specific width chosen (90 vs 79), which is dictated by the surrounding file/editor convention.

text: Document Django/CLI options that accept only a single value by writing one command invocation per value rather than repeating the option within a single invocation (which parsers may silently ignore or mishandle).
reason: Some CLI parsers do not support multiple occurrences of an option; repeating it can cause incorrect behavior or silently drop values, so documentation must reflect supported usage.
common_pattern: Correct/proper usage of Django management commands — avoiding misuse, string-based flag parsing, and redundant wrappers instead of leveraging built-in behavior directly.

text: Before adding or modifying copyright or license headers for third-party or in-kind contributions, confirm with the appropriate rights holder or legal authority who owns the copyright and what license applies; do not add 'All rights reserved' unless legal counsel confirms it is required.
reason: Prevents misattribution, incorrect relicensing, and unintended legal consequences when contributor-owned code may have separate copyright or licensing terms.
common_pattern: Copyright and license header changes require explicit legal/rights-holder confirmation regarding ownership, licensing, and unnecessary legal phrases such as 'All rights reserved'.

text: When documenting Django's calendar-versioning migration, map old and new formats by release type at matching granularity: feature releases use the base identifier (old `A.B` ↔ new `YYYY`) and patch releases append the patch number (old `A.B.C` ↔ new `YYYY.N`). Do not label feature releases as `YYYY.0` or `YYYY.N`, and use optional-component notation like `YYYY[.N]` rather than a fixed concrete pattern.
reason: Prevents readers from inferring an extra version segment or falsely equating feature releases with patch releases, keeping the analogy between the two schemes correct.
common_pattern: Django's calendar-versioning migration (PR#2733): documenting and implementing the mapping between the old A.B/A.B.C scheme and the new YYYY/YYYY.N scheme. Three related but distinct sub-patterns: (1) release documentation must map old↔new formats by release type at matching granularity, (2) version-format predicates should use semantic numeric comparisons, and (3) predicates should be named after the versioning scheme, not the current cadence.

text: When using Django's `QuerySet.delete()`, do not label the returned count as the number of primary model instances; it is the total number of deleted objects across all cascaded models. Either reword user-facing output as 'objects deleted' or compute the primary-model count separately (e.g., via `qs.count()` before deletion or from the deletion summary dict).
reason: The returned count from `delete()` includes cascaded related rows (e.g., `User.objects.filter(...).delete()` returns a count that includes `RegistrationProfile` rows), so labeling it as a user count is misleading.
common_pattern: Correctly interpret and handle Django `QuerySet.delete()` semantics in management commands: the returned count includes cascaded objects, and a single `ProtectedError` aborts the entire bulk deletion unless handled per-record.

text: When generating release documentation URLs, use the feature version as the docs path segment and preserve the release-note path convention: patch releases use `/en/{feature_version}/releases/{full_version}/`, while pre-releases use `/en/{feature_version}/releases/{feature_version}/`.
reason: Matches existing URL behavior for versions such as 5.2, 6.0, and 6.1, and avoids 404s for calendar-versioned releases.
common_pattern: Django documentation templates should not hardcode or naively derive version/language identifiers; instead they should use context variables, purpose-built version objects, or version-aware URL patterns so documentation links, labels, and canonical metadata stay accurate across versions and locales. One sub-pattern covers release-notes URL path conventions.

text: In user-facing template copy, use the objective-case relative pronoun 'whom' (not the subject-case 'who') when the pronoun functions as the object of its clause, and update translatable strings accordingly when this is flagged in review.
reason: Public-facing documentation and page copy should be grammatically correct and polished; the reviewer explicitly requested 'whom' where the referent is the object of the clause.
common_pattern: Both generalizations are rephrasings of the same grammatical rule: use the objective-case relative pronoun 'whom' (not 'who') in user-facing template copy when the pronoun is the object of its clause, and update translatable strings when review flags this.

text: In setup documentation showing system config file examples (e.g., /etc/hosts), clearly distinguish new entries the reader must add from default/pre-existing entries: state that the snippet is a new line to add rather than complete file contents, and list user-added entries on separate lines from defaults.
reason: Prevents readers from duplicating default entries, mistakenly modifying existing lines, and being confused about whether a snippet is additive or the complete file.
common_pattern: Documentation of config-file setup steps must clearly separate reader-added entries from pre-existing defaults, and edits should be minimal when the surrounding prose is already clear.

text: When existing explanatory prose already clearly describes a setup action, update only the example or code block rather than rewording the prose.
reason: Reduces documentation churn and preserves already-clear explanations.
common_pattern: Documentation of config-file setup steps must clearly separate reader-added entries from pre-existing defaults, and edits should be minimal when the surrounding prose is already clear.

text: In templates, place shared context (including plurality and count) in section headings or labels, and keep list items concise without repeating that context or stating counts that contradict the list.
reason: Reduces redundant UI copy, improves scannability, and keeps public-facing content accurate and consistent with the actual number of listed items.
common_pattern: Template/UI sections that list multiple items should let the section heading or label carry shared context, while list-item copy stays concise and avoids repeating that context or introducing contradictory count/plurality information.

text: In translation source catalogs (`locale/*/LC_MESSAGES/*.po`), preserve `#:` source-location reference comments (`#: file:line`) so translators see code context. Regenerate with `makemessages` without `--no-location` (do not strip locations), and delete those location comments only from the Transifex-generated translation output.
reason: Location comments help translators find the original strings, but are noise in generated output; the project convention is to keep them in the source only.
common_pattern: Translation (i18n) catalog workflow for this project: preserve `#:` source-location comments in PO source files while stripping them from Transifex-generated output, and keep both source and translated `.po` catalogs in version control with README instructions to commit them.

text: In contributor biographies (e.g., fundraising/index.html), list only current project affiliations and roles; omit incidental location-specific qualifiers (such as 'Django Girls <city>') and outdated affiliations the person is no longer active in.
reason: Keeps biographies accurate, concise, and respectful to current maintainers by avoiding outdated credit or irrelevant location detail.
common_pattern: Contributor biographies should stay focused on current, relevant project affiliations and omit incidental or outdated personal/project details.

text: Prefer a single source of truth for documentation and configuration; avoid creating or maintaining duplicated copies (including standalone change-tracking/changelog pages that duplicate version-control history). When content or configuration must be copied from an upstream/external source, keep the local copy synchronized with that source. In particular, when README.rst, release checklists, or other docs reproduce content maintained in django/django's canonical documentation (e.g., coding-style, how-to-release.txt), either match the upstream wording exactly or make the corresponding upstream change as well. Additionally, add an inline comment at the copy site naming the exact source.
reason: Prevents documentation/config drift, avoids redundant process artifacts, and makes future re-synchronization discoverable. Local edits to copies of Django's own docs can create unnecessary divergence from the authoritative source and lead to incorrect contribution/release steps.
scope: global; especially documentation and configuration copied from upstream/external sources such as django/django canonical documentation
common_pattern: Avoid duplicating authoritative content or configuration; prefer a single source of truth, and when copying from an external/upstream source is unavoidable, keep the copy synchronized and document its provenance.

text: Custom QuerySet/Manager methods should include a docstring describing the annotation, filtering, or transformation they apply.
reason: Custom queryset chains are opaque; docstrings make behavior (e.g., which field is annotated) discoverable without reading the method body.
common_pattern: Django ORM organization: model-specific query logic belongs on custom Manager/QuerySet classes rather than staticmethods, standalone utils, or inline in views — plus related conventions for accessing and documenting those managers.

text: In Django templates, use Django template comments (`{# ... #}` or `{% comment %}...{% endcomment %}`) instead of HTML comments for maintainer-only notes, placeholder content, or example markup, since template comments are stripped from the rendered artifact. When such a comment documents a reusable or overridable markup pattern/block, include a copy/paste-able skeleton of the expected nested markup (wrapper element with id, nested content element with class), keeping the actual block content empty or minimal.
reason: Template comments keep guidance inline for future maintainers without leaking comments or placeholder markup into rendered output; a concrete skeleton makes the pattern unambiguous and easy to copy/paste/edit rather than reconstruct from prose.
common_pattern: Conventions for Django/template comments: use template comments (not HTML comments) so maintainer-only notes and example markup are stripped from rendered output, and keep those comments meaningful, concise, and structural (skeletons showing expected markup).

text: Keep comments meaningful and concise across code and templates: explain only non-obvious intent, rationale, constraints, magic values, external-format prefixes, or key invariants. Do not leave empty comments (`{##}`, `{#  #}`) or verbose explanations, and remove comments that merely restate the code, a well-named variable, or change history already captured by git blame/commit messages. When a non-obvious value or prefix exists, add a short inline comment explaining why.
reason: Redundant, empty, verbose, and change-log-style comments add noise, become stale, and obscure the code's real intent; reserving comments for non-obvious information keeps them useful and maintainable.
common_pattern: Comment hygiene: comments should carry information the code cannot (non-obvious intent, constraints, magic values), be placed with the code they explain, and follow standard syntax. Six of nine generalizations converge on the 'do not restate / do not document change history' half, and one (Gen 7) supplies the complementary 'do document non-obvious magic values' half.

text: Public-facing release documentation and roadmap content — supported-versions/roadmap tables (including djangoproject/templates/releases/download.html), release blog posts, graphs, and generated roadmap pages — must be accurate and consistent: (1) release and end-of-support dates must match the official release schedule and be updated to the same value in every public-facing listing when they change; (2) table rows must be structurally complete (one cell per header column, one row per currently supported and planned release series), and dynamic values such as the latest micro release must be rendered with `{% get_latest_micro_release '<series>' %}` rather than hardcoded; and (3) release entries, schedules, dates, and release messaging must be derived from structured version parameters/metadata (e.g., first release version/year-month, `is_year_version`) instead of static JSON release lists or hardcoded relative timing phrases.
reason: Stale or inconsistent dates, hardcoded versions, malformed rows, or static release lists mislead users about release and support timelines; deriving from structured metadata keeps public listings accurate, complete, and consistent across releases.
scope: project-wide release documentation and roadmap generation/templates (including djangoproject/templates/releases/download.html)
common_pattern: All generalizations concern the correctness and consistency of public-facing Django release/support lifecycle documentation (primarily `djangoproject/templates/releases/download.html` and the release blog posts): accurate release/EOL dates, complete and self-consistent table rows, dynamic rather than hardcoded version values, and consistent LTS labeling across surfaces.

text: In user-facing documentation, release notes, README/support-policy pages, templates, and source-code comments, keep references concrete and current: refer to current/latest languages and runtimes without redundant major-version qualifiers; remove references to unsupported versions or deleted APIs/symbols; and avoid relative terms such as 'older', 'newer', 'legacy', or 'current' unless anchored to a concrete version, date, release, or condition. In user-facing documentation and release notes, also prefer concise phrasing by removing redundant qualifiers or modifiers when the meaning remains clear (e.g., use 'support periods' rather than 'support periods of individual release series').
reason: Keeps documentation copy tight and readable while preventing references from becoming misleading as versions, APIs, or context change.
scope: documentation, release notes, README/support-policy pages, templates, source-code comments
common_pattern: Avoid documentation and comment references that become stale or ambiguous over time, such as redundant version qualifiers, references to unsupported versions or deleted APIs, and unanchored relative temporal terms.

text: When updating Django community/ecosystem resource listing templates (e.g. `djangoproject/templates/aggregator/ecosystem.html` and `base_community.html`), keep entries curated and correctly categorized: add each resource to the existing categorized `<ul>`/`<dd>` list that matches its type, preserve/restore surrounding semantic markup when editing, use the canonical link and a brief description if the surrounding entries use one, include only third-party packages that support the current Django release and have clear/trustworthy documentation, and place packages on track for partial integration into Django more prominently than generic utilities/miscellaneous entries.
reason: These listing pages are organized into categorized resource lists and endorse packages/resources on behalf of the community, so entries must be placed in the right section, remain trustworthy and current, and be surfaced according to relevance.
scope: Django community/ecosystem resource listing templates such as `djangoproject/templates/aggregator/ecosystem.html` and `djangoproject/templates/base_community.html`
common_pattern: Curation and organization conventions for Django community/ecosystem resource listing templates

text: Add a comment explaining why a migration is intentionally empty or has no operations (e.g., pointing to git history for removed logic) so future readers aren't confused.
reason: An empty migration without explanation confuses future readers; a comment preserves intent and context.
common_pattern: Django migration best practices — managing the content, naming, purpose, and PR-scope of migration files so migration history stays intentional and clean

text: Add `help_text` (using `_()` for translation) to Django model fields whose meaning, business constraint, public-display behavior, or selection/precedence logic is not obvious from the field name and type — e.g. a flag enforcing an exclusivity rule like 'only one record may be active at a time', a field shown publicly on the site, a when-to-set condition, or an ambiguous boolean/status label (include a concrete example value). Write the `help_text` as a concise, grammatical, self-contained user-facing sentence that describes the field's effect once, avoiding duplicated or self-referential phrasing (e.g. 'make this entry allow this entry to…'). Keep numeric guidance accurate: use correct SI unit symbols (e.g. 'MB' not 'Mb') and external platforms' officially documented values (e.g. canonical sharing-card dimensions), since these strings are shown directly to admin users and drive their behavior. Place field-specific behavioral explanations in the field's `help_text`, not in utility-function comments.
reason: Field-level `help_text` documents non-obvious semantics at the point of definition, surfacing constraints and public-facing behavior in the Django admin/forms for future maintainers and non-developer domain users. It is less likely to drift than comments elsewhere, but because it is displayed directly in the admin UI and forms, awkward, redundant, or factually incorrect wording reduces clarity, misinforms users about limits/constraints, and degrades the generated admin interface.
scope: global for Django model field help_text
common_pattern: All generalizations concern Django model field `help_text` as user-facing documentation. Two complementary sub-patterns emerge: (1) WHEN to add help_text — for fields whose semantics, constraints, public-display behavior, or selection/precedence logic are not obvious from the field name/type; and (2) HOW to write it — concise, grammatical, non-redundant, with correct units and accurate externally-documented values.

text: In Django documentation templates and templatetags, avoid hardcoding version or language values (such as `1.8`, `en`, or `stable`) for links, canonical/hreflang metadata, or version labels. Use context variables or purpose-built version objects instead: use the current page version for page-specific links, use the `stable` alias for stable-docs links and resolve it via `DocumentRelease.objects.current_version()` when needed, and use `preview.feature_version` rather than slicing raw version strings.
reason: Hardcoded or naively sliced values produce stale or incorrect documentation links and labels, break URL reversal for pre-release/calendar versions (e.g. `2028a1` sliced to `202`), and can cause `NoReverseMatch` or locale/version mismatches in canonical metadata.
scope: Django documentation templates and templatetags, especially release/download and canonical/hreflang URL generation
common_pattern: Django documentation templates should not hardcode or naively derive version/language identifiers; instead they should use context variables, purpose-built version objects, or version-aware URL patterns so documentation links, labels, and canonical metadata stay accurate across versions and locales. One sub-pattern covers release-notes URL path conventions.

text: Do not put maintainer/contributor-facing notes in `.well-known/security.txt`; place them in `SECURITY.md` or the contributor README. If `security.txt` embeds a long-lived external reference such as an encryption key fingerprint, document or link its canonical source there so it can be refreshed safely.
reason: `.well-known/security.txt` is aimed at external security reporters, so maintainer-facing update notes placed there are unlikely to reach their intended audience.
common_pattern: Maintaining `.well-known/security.txt` as externally focused, internally consistent security-reporting metadata, with separate maintainer-facing documentation and explicit scope-specific reporting contacts.

text: In `.github/SECURITY.md`, security reporting guidance must be concrete and unambiguous: each instruction should state a specific, actionable expectation a reporter can follow, and the policy must not make fixed response-time commitments (e.g. acknowledgement "within 3 working days") unless the team can reliably honor them.
reason: Vague guidance confuses reporters, and self-imposed hard deadlines borrowed from other projects create obligations and expectations the team may be unable to meet, lowering report quality and consistency.
common_pattern: Authoring guidelines for `.github/SECURITY.md` (GitHub security policy documentation) — ensuring the policy is concrete, accurate, and tailored to the project's real capabilities and platform.

text: Tailor `.github/SECURITY.md` to the project's actual platform and operating model: for GitHub-hosted repositories, recommend GitHub's private vulnerability reporting (e.g. `security/advisories/new`) as a secure channel when the team can receive it; for services/websites with no release cycle, base public-disclosure triggers on compromise of user data rather than software releases; and prefer established terminology such as "security defect" over "security bug"/"security issue".
reason: The policy should reflect what the team can actually support and how the project is delivered — recommending a channel the team can't decrypt, using release-oriented disclosure language for a service, or using non-standard terms all mislead reporters and reduce consistency.
scope: security policy documentation for a specific project (`.github/SECURITY.md`)
common_pattern: Authoring guidelines for `.github/SECURITY.md` (GitHub security policy documentation) — ensuring the policy is concrete, accurate, and tailored to the project's real capabilities and platform.

text:
PO files under `dashboard/locale/*/LC_MESSAGES/django.po` must use the project's standard header instead of gettext-generated placeholders. Use exactly:
```
# Copyright (C) Django Software Foundation and contributors
# This file is distributed under the same license as the djangoproject.com source files.
```
To keep generated PO headers consistent and avoid hand-editing each locale file, configure this header in the translation platform's project-wide header template (e.g. Transifex project settings) so newly generated PO files include it automatically.
reason: Keeps translation files consistent with the project's docs PO files and avoids shipping placeholder copyright, license, or attribution text such as `SOME DESCRIPTIVE TITLE.` or `YEAR THE PACKAGE'S COPYRIGHT HOLDER`. Configuring the platform header template avoids repeated manual edits across locale files.
common_pattern: Translation (.po) files in this repository must carry the project's standard copyright/license header — ideally by configuring the header template in the translation platform so generated files get it automatically — rather than gettext placeholder metadata.

text: When styling or scripting DOM elements, reuse existing selectors and hooks instead of adding redundant classes, attributes, or data-testids: target an element’s existing unique ID or a class that the JavaScript already depends on. For elements expected to appear multiple times or that need shared behavior, use a class selector (or a unique ID per element) rather than a shared ID — e.g. in djangoproject frontend JavaScript (`djangoproject/static/js/mod/*`), query floating documentation warning banners by the shared `.doc-floating-warning` class rather than variant-specific IDs like `#dev-warning` or `#outdated-warning`, so shared behavior (such as layout offset calculations) applies to all banner variants. For DOM lookups by ID, prefer `getElementById('id')` as the direct, faster API, and keep the element-query style consistent within a given file instead of arbitrarily mixing `querySelector` and `getElementById`.
reason: Existing IDs and classes are sufficient, semantically meaningful hooks; redundant hooks pollute markup and can drift. Conversely, relying on an ID for repeatable elements produces invalid HTML and ambiguous selection. A class selector covers all current and future banner variants, whereas an ID selector silently misses banners, breaking shared behavior like height/offset computation. `getElementById` is the specialized, marginally faster API for ID lookups, while local consistency improves readability and refactor-safety.
common_pattern: Selector strategy for DOM elements: reuse existing semantic hooks (unique IDs, existing classes) instead of adding redundant classes/attributes, and choose ID vs. class based on whether the element is unique or recurring/shared.

text: When normalizing text by stripping or replacing many characters, use a single regex substitution (e.g., `re.sub`, compiled if reused) instead of repeated `.replace()` calls or loops over punctuation/character sets. In request middleware, minimize per-request overhead by applying the same approach to URL path normalization rather than conditional branching with split/join; also wrap the default response call in a try block and fall back to normalization and redirect only when a 404 (`Http404`) is raised, so the common case stays on the fast path.
reason: Consolidates replacement logic into one pass, improving readability, maintainability, and performance. Middleware runs on every request, so designing the common case as the fast path reduces CPU overhead.
common_pattern: Consolidating repeated text-normalization and regex logic into a single reusable construct rather than duplicating operations or literals.

text: When making a change that applies to a repeated pattern—whether fixing formatting, spelling, localization, date formats, HTML structure, adopting a preferred syntax/convention, or introducing a reusable abstraction for a repeated literal, translated string fragment, or hardcoded assumption—apply the change consistently to every occurrence within the relevant scope (at minimum the affected file/change set; for conventions or reusable abstractions, search the PR/project or entire codebase as appropriate). Do not update only the flagged instance.
reason: Partial changes leave inconsistent duplicates, mixed conventions, untranslatable strings, and the same defect elsewhere, causing follow-up cleanup and undermining the intended fix or abstraction.
common_pattern: When a review identifies a needed fix (localization, formatting, or markup) to a repeated pattern in a template file, the fix must be applied to every occurrence of that pattern in the file, not only the reported instance.

text: When adding or modifying lines in an existing file, match the surrounding file's formatting style rather than introducing a new convention. This includes consistent indentation (use the file's indentation width; consistent tabs/spaces, no mixed), blank-line usage (avoid extra blank lines, e.g. after class declarations or around newly added settings/top-level assignments), naming, spacing, and formatting of similar statements. In SCSS stylesheets specifically, use 4 spaces (not tabs), place a space before an opening `{`, separate rule sections with a single blank line (not two), and close every opened block with a matching `}`. In JavaScript files under `djangoproject/static/js/`, use the file's indentation width without tabs/mixed indentation, follow its naming style, keep short calls with simple object arguments on one line when nearby code does, and write a space before opening braces (e.g. `function() {`, not `function(){`).
reason: Consistent, local formatting keeps diffs clean, avoids lint/style failures and tab/space rendering differences, prevents unbalanced braces, and avoids noisy formatting churn.
common_pattern: All generalizations require contributors to preserve the established code style of existing JavaScript files rather than introducing their own formatting, naming, or spacing conventions.

text: Avoid unnecessary indirection from single-use values: inline one-off local variables and constants that are referenced only once at their use site, and inline trivial single-use boolean variables directly into their condition. For derived boolean properties, return the combined condition directly, composing existing boolean helper properties rather than re-checking their underlying fields or using nested if/fallthrough. If a single-use variable is genuinely needed, give it a concise name reflecting its immediate use rather than a verbose descriptive name.
reason: Single-use named variables and boolean indirection add visual noise without enabling reuse; direct expressions keep related logic close, reduce redundant branching and null-check duplication, and keep boolean properties consistent with their source-of-truth helpers.
common_pattern: Avoid unnecessary named indirection for values that are only used once — inline single-use variables/constants at their use site, and when a temporary name is unavoidable, keep it short and reflective of its immediate use.

text: For Python multi-line function/method calls and collection literals (lists, dicts, tuples), use a hanging indent: keep the opening delimiter at the end of the assignment/call line, put one item per line indented one level, include a trailing comma after the final item, and place the closing delimiter on its own line aligned with the line that opened the construct. If the expression fits on one line, keep it on one line; when it does not, avoid aligning continuation arguments under the opening parenthesis. Apply this consistently to Django model declarations: keep short field definitions and `Meta` options (such as `indexes`) on a single line when they fit within the line-length limit; when a declaration must wrap across multiple lines, use hanging indents and match existing multi-line model declarations in the same file.
reason: This preserves intentional multi-line formatting, avoids formatter collapse, produces cleaner future diffs and fewer merge conflicts, reduces visual noise for short declarations, and keeps Python and Django model formatting visually clear and consistent with Black-style conventions.
common_pattern: Python multi-line formatting conventions for function calls and collection literals, centered on Black-style hanging indentation, trailing commas, and closing delimiters placed on their own line.

text: Remove template conditionals (`{% if %}`) that guard against states that cannot occur—such as dropped features or values guaranteed by upstream validation—so templates do not contain dead branches or misleading fallback rendering.
reason: Dead conditional branches in templates add confusion and maintenance burden. Templates should assume valid data when upstream logic guarantees it.
common_pattern: Template conditionals should be removed when the guarded state cannot occur, whether because the feature was dropped or because upstream validation guarantees the value.

text: Use standard or project-level timezone-aware utilities consistently: prefer `datetime.timezone.utc` over `get_fixed_timezone(0)` for UTC, and use the project's timezone-aware date helper (e.g., `timezone_today()`) instead of `date.today()` in code and tests.
reason: These choices avoid naive datetime handling, reduce unnecessary helper imports, and keep timezone behavior consistent with production code, preventing timezone-dependent test failures.
scope: global for UTC representation; project-specific (members app) and tests for date helper
common_pattern: Prefer standard or project-level timezone-aware utilities over naive or ad-hoc timezone/date constructs to ensure consistency and clarity.

text: In SCSS, when child selectors share a parent selector (e.g. `#billboard div`, `table.docutils td`), nest them inside the parent block instead of repeating the parent prefix or creating separate top-level classes for each element; group container and descendant element styles under a single parent selector.
reason: Nesting co-locates related styles, mirrors the DOM hierarchy, reduces selector duplication/class proliferation, and improves readability and maintainability.
common_pattern: Project-wide SCSS/CSS stylesheet style conventions covering whitespace/formatting and selector nesting structure

text: When building a string from multiple dynamic parts, use flat, single-style interpolation rather than nesting interpolations of the same style or wrapping an entire concatenation expression inside one placeholder. Interpolate each dynamic value individually — e.g. `f"{a}{b}"` / `${a}${b}` instead of `f"{f'{a}'}{b}"` or `${a + b}` — or split into intermediate statements.
reason: Nested same-style interpolations and concatenation expressions embedded inside a placeholder are harder to read and more error-prone than flat, per-value interpolation.
common_pattern: String interpolation style: avoid nested or mixed-style interpolations, and interpolate each dynamic value individually instead of wrapping concatenation/compound expressions inside a single placeholder.

text: When composing the system font stack (e.g., the `sans-serif` mixin in `djangoproject/scss/_utils.scss`), list platform-specific system fonts (`-apple-system`, `BlinkMacSystemFont`, `"Segoe UI"`, `Roboto`) before `system-ui`, include common Linux families (`"Oxygen-Sans"`, `"Ubuntu"`, `"Cantarell"`, `"Noto Sans"`), and terminate with generic families plus emoji fonts. Do not place `system-ui` first.
reason: `system-ui` first causes severe font-rendering problems for certain languages (Django ticket #33878), and omitting Linux families means Linux users (a large share of Django devs/visitors) get inconsistent rendering. Loading `-apple-system` first alone is also insufficient because it is Apple-specific.
common_pattern: Font-stack configuration correctness: composing CSS font stacks that render the intended font across platforms/languages, and preserving font variants when changing how webfonts are loaded.

text: When replacing or removing a font-loading mechanism (e.g., swapping `webfontloader` for Google Fonts `<link>` tags, or dropping a Google Fonts `<link>` from `base.html`), verify the replacement supplies exactly the weights and styles the removed source requested (parse variants like `ital,wght@0,300;0,400;0,700;1,400;1,700`), and prefer the official Google Fonts embed code.
reason: The variant list encodes the exact font weights/italics the site depends on; missing variants cause silent browser synthesis or fallback, producing visual regressions in styles that use those weights/styles.
common_pattern: Font-stack configuration correctness: composing CSS font stacks that render the intended font across platforms/languages, and preserving font variants when changing how webfonts are loaded.

text: Drive both the UI affordance that advertises a keyboard shortcut (e.g., placeholder text) and the shortcut's registration from the same visibility/support predicate so unsupported shortcuts are never advertised.
reason: Avoids showing users a shortcut hint that cannot actually work in their environment.
common_pattern: Platform-appropriate and consistent keyboard shortcut implementation and display in UI

text: Treat inline code suggestions as actionable review requests: an empty suggestion means delete the selected lines, and a concrete suggestion such as a simpler equivalent form means either adopt it or explain why the existing code is required.
reason: Review suggestions embed reviewer intent. Ignoring a suggestion or treating it only as a question leaves the intent unresolved and can contradict the requested change.
common_pattern: Inline code suggestions in review comments are actionable directives, not merely questions: an empty suggestion requests deletion, while a concrete suggestion requests adoption or justification of the proposed change.

text: Use `const` by default and `let` only when a binding is reassigned in JavaScript; avoid `var`. Use `const` for UPPER_CASE constants and for simple conditional value assignments (prefer a ternary assigned to `const` over an `if` that mutates `var`/`let`).
reason: `const`/`let` provide block scoping, communicate mutability intent, and avoid `var` hoisting pitfalls. Using `const` for constants and conditional assignments prevents accidental reassignment and is idiomatic JavaScript.
common_pattern: Modern JavaScript variable declaration and naming conventions, primarily preferring `const`/`let` over `var` with correct mutability, plus camelCase naming. Most generalizations converge on declaration style; one is a distinct naming sub-pattern.

text: Style placeholder text with a single global rule that groups the standard `::placeholder` and vendor-prefixed variants (`::-webkit-input-placeholder`, `:-ms-input-placeholder`, `::-moz-placeholder`, `:-moz-placeholder`), uses theme CSS variables such as `var(--body-fg)` instead of hard-coded color literals, and avoids per-input-type placeholder selectors that duplicate styling already covered by the broader global rule.
reason: This consolidates placeholder styling, ensures older browser engines apply the style, and keeps placeholder colors consistent with the active theme and global palette while avoiding redundant maintenance.
common_pattern: CSS placeholder styling conventions: consolidate placeholder styling into a global rule, support browser vendor prefixes, and use theme CSS variables instead of hard-coded colors.

text: Decide helper placement by coupling, not usage count: colocate domain-specific code with its single consumer (e.g., a one-off helper defined next to its call site, or a form in `accounts.forms`) and only extract it into a shared `utils`/dedicated app when reuse actually emerges. Exception: code that generically extends a framework (not domain logic) belongs in a shared `contrib/<framework>/` package from the start, even if currently used in only one place.
reason: Reduces indirection and premature abstraction while preserving a clean boundary between generic framework extensions and domain-specific logic.
common_pattern: Abstraction/placement threshold for helpers: don't extract into shared modules/apps prematurely — BUT the deciding axis is not usage count alone, it's whether the code is domain-specific (colocate with its single consumer) or a generic framework extension (belongs in a shared contrib/<framework>/ package even with one consumer).

text: When modifying shared/global styles, audit all consumers and scope overrides to the specific instance rather than altering the shared class, unless the change is intentionally global and verified safe.
reason: Prevents unintended regressions in other pages or components that depend on the shared style.
common_pattern: CSS organization and class hygiene in djangoproject.com: centralize styles in project SCSS/shared stylesheets, use only defined/reusable classes, avoid inline or dead/legacy styling, and scope shared-style changes safely.

text: In SCSS/CSS, reference existing shared color tokens (SCSS variables from `_utils.scss`/`_dark-mode.scss` or CSS custom properties such as `var(--white-color)`) instead of hardcoding hex colors; when changing a theme color, update all corresponding light/dark-mode declarations and reuse existing similar colors rather than adding new ones.
reason: Centralizes the color palette, supports theming and dark mode consistently, avoids duplicate/magic color values, and prevents dark-mode visual drift when base colors change.
scope: project SCSS/CSS stylesheets, especially djangoproject.com theming files
common_pattern: Use shared SCSS/CSS color tokens instead of hardcoded colors, and keep light/dark theme color declarations synchronized across the project.

reason: Keeps markup style consistent and aligns with the project's preferred HTML syntax.
common_pattern: Django template formatting and markup style conventions

text: In Django templates, break `{% if %}...{% else %}...{% endif %}` blocks across multiple lines rather than keeping the whole conditional on one line; when only an attribute value is conditional, use an inline `{% if %}` inside the attribute instead of duplicating the entire HTML element in separate branches.
reason: Multi-line conditionals are easier to read and diff, and inline conditionals avoid duplicated markup that can diverge.
common_pattern: Django template formatting and markup style conventions

text: Do not append `|safe` after `|escape` in Django templates; `|escape` already marks its output as safe.
reason: The `|safe` filter is redundant and may imply that escaped output still needs explicit safe marking.
common_pattern: Django template formatting and markup style conventions

text: Scope layout-affecting CSS properties (e.g., `overflow-wrap: break-word`) to the specific component/block selectors that need them rather than applying them to broad selectors like `body`.
reason: Global application of these properties can cause unintended wrapping and layout changes in unrelated parts of the site; scoping limits side effects to known, tested blocks and reduces unexpected regressions.
common_pattern: Both generalizations state the same CSS design principle: layout-affecting properties like `overflow-wrap: break-word` should be scoped to the narrowest component/block selector that needs them, not applied globally (e.g., on `body`). They are rephrasings from the same review discussion, so this is a convergent cluster.
